videos.title: Nancy Grace to Brandon Tatum: “Are You Even Listening?”
videos.description:
Nancy Grace questioned Brandon Tatum’s listening skills during their discussion of the Sea Tow dispatch call connected to the Nolan Wells case.

In this video, I analyze that exchange and the larger logical issue surrounding Brandon’s interpretation of the recording:

Does hearing—or failing to hear—a particular phrase establish what happened?

Audio interpretation is not the same thing as verified fact. A conclusion cannot rest solely on what one person believes they heard, especially when the recording contains overlapping voices, background noise, and disputed dialogue.

This analysis is not a declaration of guilt or innocence. It is an examination of whether the conclusions being presented logically follow from the available evidence.

videos.title: Did Nolan Wells’ Family Lie? Brandon Tatum’s Argument Falls Apart
videos.description:
YouTube Description

Brandon Tatum claims Nolan Wells’ family may have been “busted” in a massive lie.

But the evidence he presents does not establish that conclusion.

In this response, I examine the call logs, the statements attributed to Nolan’s mother, the messages from other parents, and Brandon’s claim that the family’s refusal to communicate proves dishonesty or a lack of interest in finding the truth.

Correcting an earlier statement is not automatically proof of a lie.

Receiving a message is not the same as having a meaningful conversation.

A parent declining private contact during an active investigation does not prove that parent is dishonest, malicious, or uninterested in learning what happened to their child.

And the fact that someone contacted Nolan’s mother at 11:07 p.m. does not erase the legitimate questions about what happened before that call, why Nolan was left behind, who last saw him, or what occurred afterward.

This video also examines:

Why a correction is not necessarily a “massive lie”
The difference between attempted contact and an actual conversation
Brandon’s assumptions about how grieving parents should behave
Why contacting another parent does not establish innocence
The misuse of call logs as proof of an entire narrative
The claim that having many people on Horn Island eliminates foul play
The distinction between evidence, interpretation, and conclusion
Why every reasonable possibility must remain open

I am not declaring Warren or his friends guilty.

I am not declaring Nolan’s family beyond criticism.

I am applying the same evidentiary standard to everyone.

Brandon titled his video “Did Nolan Wells’ Family JUST GET BUSTED In MASSIVE LIE?” But a provocative title is not an argument, and suspicion is not proof.

Some people do not investigate cases.

They investigate whether the case fits their worldview.

That is not justice.

That is ideology.

Every reasonable possibility stays on the table until the evidence takes it off.

videos.title: Brandon Tatum’s Part 2: More Claims, Still Not Proof
videos.description:
In this video, I respond to Part 2 of Brandon Tatum's investigation into the Nolan Wells case.

Unlike many reactions online, this is not a personal attack on Brandon Tatum, Ben Crump, or any witness involved.

This is an examination of reasoning.

In Part 1, I argued that witness testimony is evidence—but it is not proof by itself.

In Part 2, Brandon presents additional claims about Horn Island, the number of boats, the crowds, the phones, and the timeline. Some of that information is valuable. But the central question remains:

Do the conclusions actually follow from the evidence?

That is what we examine in this video.

We discuss:

Whether testimony is being confused with proof.
Whether a crowded island eliminates other possibilities.
The logical difference between plausibility and certainty.
Why corroboration matters in every investigation.
Why one corrected fact does not automatically resolve an entire case.

My commitment remains the same:

One standard.

Whether the speaker is Brandon Tatum...

Ben Crump...

law enforcement...

the media...

or anyone else.
